title: The Gang Suppression Force in Haiti: A New Peacekeeping Template?
summary: Maya and Daniel unpack a November 2026 policy brief from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime by Sophie Rutenbar examining Haiti's Gang Suppression Force. They explore why this hybrid, non-UN-led peace enforcement model was created, the logistical and strategic hurdles it faces, and what it reveals about the future of international interventions against powerful criminal groups.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome to the podcast. Today we are digging into a fascinating new policy brief from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, or GI-TOC. It is titled A Model for Future Peace Operations? Lessons from the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti, written by Sophie Rutenbar.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And for anyone watching international security, peace operations, or organized crime, this is really critical reading. We are talking about the Gang Suppression Force, or GSF, which replaced the Multinational Security Support Mission in Haiti.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. And Rutenbar is asking a fundamental question: is this strange, hybrid mission just an emergency compromise cobbled together because traditional multilateralism is stuck, or is it actually becoming a template for how the world deals with armed criminal gangs and state collapse?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: The opening anecdote of the report really sets the stakes, doesn't it? It just hits you immediately.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It really does. On October 18, 2026, four Salvadoran soldiers serving with the GSF disappeared in gang-controlled territory in metropolitan Port-au-Prince while returning from an errand. At the time of writing, their fate is still completely unknown. And that happened more than a year after the UN Security Council authorized this force to neutralize Haiti's gangs.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It captures the stark reality on the ground. Despite an international deployment, criminal groups still control most of the territory where the force operates. What are the broader conditions in Haiti right now according to the brief?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: They are grim. One in ten Haitians is internally displaced. More than half the population faces acute food insecurity. And the political timeline keeps slipping. Elections were originally planned for August 2026, then moved to December 13, and now they have been pushed all the way back to July 18, 2027 for the first round, with a run-off slated for October 4, 2027.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So against that backdrop, let us step back and look at what the GSF actually is. How did it come into being?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It was established by UN Security Council Resolution 2793 on September 30, 2025, succeeding the MSS. Then, on September 29, 2026, Resolution 2829 renewed its mandate for six months, until March 31, 2027. It is led by Special Representative Jack Christofides and Force Commander Major General Erdenebat Batsuuri.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And how is it fundamentally different from the MSS that came before it?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: In several crucial ways. The MSS was primarily a police mission, and it really struggled, fielding only about 1 000 officers. The GSF is authorized for up to 5 500 military and police personnel, plus 50 civilian staff. And crucially, it is mostly military personnel, especially in its early deployment phases. Its primary mandated task is counter-gang operations to neutralize, isolate, and deter gangs.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So it is firmly at the peace enforcement end of the spectrum.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Very much so. The mandate gives it the option to operate independently or jointly with Haitian security actors as it sees fit. It is also tasked with securing critical infrastructure, building the capacity of Haitian forces, and helping create security conditions conducive to elections.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Yet, even though the UN Security Council authorized it, the UN does not actually run it. That is the hybrid architecture Rutenbar focuses on.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. This is what she calls Challenge One: coordination and decision-making. The GSF is authorized by the UN, but it is not a UN-led peacekeeping operation. Strategic direction and oversight come from the Standing Group of Partners, or SGP, which is led by the United States with Canada, and includes countries like the Bahamas, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Jamaica.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And they had an operational task force helping get it off the ground, right?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, the Tiger Team, composed mainly of staff from the US State Department and Department of War, alongside other partners. They acted as a secretariat, identifying and preparing contingents. But to support the mission logistically, the UN created UNSOH, the United Nations Support Office in Haiti, headed by Daniela Kroslak. UNSOH became fully operational on April 1, 2026, and is funded through assessed UN contributions to handle things like bases, rations, fuel, medical support, and transport.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Wait, let's untangle that funding, because it sounds remarkably fragmented. You have assessed contributions for UNSOH, but what about the troops themselves?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Troop reimbursement is paid through a separate UN trust fund funded by voluntary donor contributions. As of September 23, 2026, that trust fund had around 200 million US dollars to pay standard UN peacekeeping reimbursement rates. Canada separately pays the salaries of the GSF civilian staff. And then there is another fund held by the Organization of American States, the OAS, for urgent operational needs that neither UNSOH nor the trust fund cover, like contracting bulldozers to smash through gang roadblocks.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And on top of that, you have BINUH, the UN Integrated Office in Haiti, leading external political engagement, plus CARICOM's Eminent Persons Group. That is an extraordinarily crowded institutional landscape.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It really is. You have the Senior Leadership Coordination Forum bringing together BINUH, UNSOH, and the GSF, meeting regularly with the Haitian prime minister. But as Rutenbar points out, managing this hybrid beast requires massive civilian liaison capacity. Yet by early October 2026, less than 30 of the GSF's planned 50 civilian positions were filled.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which brings us directly to Challenge Two: the reality of logistics and troop deployment. The mission was authorized in September 2025. Where did its actual strength stand by late October 2026?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Just over 2 000 personnel. Now, that does make it larger than the MSS ever was. But it is still well below its 5 500 ceiling, and full operational capacity is not expected before December 2026 at the earliest.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: The report compares that to MINUSTAH back in 2004. How does the timeline stack up?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It is an interesting comparison. MINUSTAH was authorized on April 30, 2004. By November 8, roughly six months in, MINUSTAH had nearly 4 500 personnel on the ground. But Rutenbar points out that MINUSTAH absorbed troops already present under the Multinational Interim Force, like Chilean soldiers, and Brazilian units were already rolling in. Plus, MINUSTAH was an established UN peacekeeping mission deploying through existing institutional machinery in a different geopolitical era.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Whereas the GSF had to invent its own procedures from scratch. What caused the actual delays?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: A cascade of administrative and logistical hurdles. First, legal status. Unlike UN staff, GSF personnel had no automatic diplomatic immunity or status. They had to negotiate an agreement with the OAS to extend OAS legal identity to civilian staff just so they could enter Haiti safely without facing legal pursuit. And while a status agreement between the GSF and Haiti was signed in late July 2026, each contributing nation still has to negotiate bilateral agreements with the Haitian government.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Then there was force generation and equipment. Pledges came in, but contingents were not as self-sufficient as planners hoped.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Not at all. A pledging conference in December 2025 gathered thousands of pledges. The contributing countries as of October 2026 are Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia, and Sri Lanka. But many units arrived without adequate gear, or with equipment completely unsuited to Haiti, like tents that could not withstand Port-au-Prince's heavy rains. UNSOH had to step in and procure missing items, or wait for donations, which were delayed because arms embargoes required end-user certificates for military or dual-use equipment.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And then the sheer cost of moving troops. That figure for the Sri Lankan contingent blew me away.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Thirty million dollars. That was the cost of a single strategic airlift to fly Sri Lankan assets into Haiti. The report notes that is ten times what it would have cost by sea. But sea transport takes six weeks or more. So you are caught between astronomical air costs or weeks of transit delays.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And once they land, they need induction training. In standard UN missions, units are supposed to arrive pre-trained. Here, they have had to spend one to two weeks doing induction training on arrival, learning to navigate urban Port-au-Prince or the rural terrain of the Artibonite department, and learning unfamiliar vehicles.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. And Rutenbar makes a sharp analytical point here: this slow roll-out does not happen in a vacuum. It actually shapes gang behavior. If terrestrial units arrive before maritime assets, gangs shift illicit activities to coastal waters. If border units are delayed, gangs reinforce positions along the border with the Dominican Republic. So rather than GSF dictating the tempo, its phased arrival causes gangs to adapt, which then forces the GSF into a reactive posture.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That leads straight into Challenge Three: mission objectives versus broader expectations. This seems like a recipe for public frustration.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It is classic mission creep pressure. In June 2026, the GSF submitted its strategy with three benchmarks to achieve by late 2028: decreasing gang territorial control, securing critical infrastructure with Haitian police and armed forces, and improving Haitian security forces' ability to contain violence. But the Haitian public and politicians expect far more.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Like securing the elections?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Precisely. The GSF is mandated to help create conditions conducive to elections, not to provide election security or run electoral operations. Yet Haitian actors constantly pressure them to announce when it will be safe enough to vote.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And then there is the pressure to protect civilians when gangs strike outside GSF operational sectors. Tell us about Kenscoff and Gros Morne.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Those two cases illustrate the dilemma perfectly. In late August 2026, gangs launched brutal attacks in Kenscoff, south of Port-au-Prince. The public demanded GSF deploy there. But GSF operational plans had assigned the south to the Haitian National Police, the HNP. The GSF did not want to disperse newly arrived troops into unfamiliar terrain. So they deployed into downtown Port-au-Prince to free up HNP units to go to Kenscoff.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: A sensible operational workaround, but hard to explain to terrified citizens.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And look at Gros Morne in Artibonite. GSF troops carried out an operation that killed three members of the Kokorat San Ras gang. Just hours later, the gang retaliated by massacring around a dozen civilians. To prevent further slaughter, the GSF felt forced to establish a permanent base near Gros Morne.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which is holding ground, something the GSF was specifically not designed to do.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. If the force answers every single emergency, it disperses its 2 000 troops, gets bogged down holding static territory, and loses its offensive momentum. But if it stays in base, it loses the trust of the population, which it desperately needs for intelligence and cooperation.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which brings us to Challenge Four: restoring security versus maintaining it. This is really about the follow-through and the Haitian state.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. Who holds the cleared ground? It has to be the Haitian National Police and the Armed Forces of Haiti, the FADH. But the HNP is fragile, under-resourced, and deeply compromised by gang penetration. The FADH is still rebuilding from a tiny officer corps. Initially, the GSF decided to conduct operations independently to prevent operational leaks. But if they operate independently, they are not building the capacity of local forces.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And what happens to the gang members who are detained or who want to surrender? Haiti's justice system was already in ruins.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: This is a massive bottleneck. Haiti's pre-trial detention rate is already over 80 percent. The planned modular detention facility for the GSF can only hold 160 individuals. That is a drop in the ocean. The transitional government did establish specialized judicial units in May 2026 for financial crimes and mass atrocities, but they take time to become operational. Meanwhile, disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration, or DDR, remains stuck in planning, waiting on funding.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us turn to the bigger picture. In the final section, Rutenbar pulls out several major lessons for the future of peace operations worldwide. What is the first takeaway?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: First, the hybrid model does not actually reduce cost or complexity; it just shifts them. Ad hoc coalitions are often sold as leaner, cheaper, and faster than UN peacekeeping. But by one US official's estimate, the US spent close to one billion dollars mounting and supporting the MSS. Moving Sri Lankan gear cost 30 million dollars. And the GSF took just as long to mobilize as MINUSTAH did twenty years ago. The costs simply moved from the UN assessment budget to bilateral donors, contributing countries, and a separate support office.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the second lesson is that these hurdles were completely predictable. Negotiating ad hoc legal statuses, vetting contingents from scratch, airlifting heavy gear <short pause> all of that could have been prepared in advance.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. If member states want to use this model again, they need pre-negotiated legal templates, rosters of pre-assessed units, pooled equipment, and standing airlift contracts. Otherwise, every hybrid mission will waste its first six to twelve months reinventing basic logistics.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What about the civilian side and the nature of the adversary?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Third, civilian capacity must deploy first, not last. You need political and communications staff on the ground before the troops arrive to manage expectations and set up coordination. Fourth, an enforcement mission is only as good as what follows it. If you do not fund detention, courts, and DDR from day one, your military victories evaporate the minute troops withdraw.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And finally, criminal gangs are fundamentally different from rebel groups or political insurgents.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, this is a core GI-TOC insight. You cannot treat criminal gangs like political insurgents who will eventually sit down for peace talks. Gangs survive on illicit revenue streams, weapons trafficking, and elite political protection. If you push them with military force, they just displace, diversify, and strike vulnerable civilians. To defeat them, you have to target the criminal economy and political patrons, not just clear city blocks.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So looking forward, the brief outlines seven concrete recommendations. What are the key priorities there?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Number one: complete the GSF deployment and sequence it strategically. Partners need to secure the airlift and equipment to reach full capacity by early 2027, prioritizing the maritime unit, military intelligence, and border management to close off gang escape and smuggling routes.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Number two: simplify coordination and staff up the civilian side, filling key posts in political affairs, human rights, and communications.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Number three: manage expectations publicly. Tell the Haitian public clearly what the GSF can and cannot do, and plan operations with civilian reprisal protection in mind, coordinating closely with HNP.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Number four: invest heavily right now in Haitian security forces, including the US-backed P4000 police initiative and FADH build-up, so they can actually hold territory.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Number five: prepare the post-operation chain. Secure multi-year donor funding for detention facilities, the new specialized judicial units, and a national DDR process. Six: target the criminal economy through intelligence on gang financing, arms trafficking networks, and UN sanctions. And seven: capture these institutional lessons so the UN and member states do not start from scratch next time.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: As Rutenbar concludes, the GSF cannot single-handedly fix Haiti, but it can buy time by providing basic protection and containing gang violence so that ordinary people can work, go to school, and eventually vote. What Haiti and its international partners do with that time will decide whether this is a genuine turning point or just another brief pause in the crisis.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: A sobering and essential analysis. The report is A Model for Future Peace Operations? Lessons from the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti by Sophie Rutenbar, published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime in November 2026. Highly recommended reading. Thanks for tuning in, and we will catch you next time.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Until next time.
